sourceNote: Synthetic stress-test case in the Marketplace / Platform (B2B) domain, built with realistic, internally-consistent SaaS metrics (ARR, growth, churn, NRR, CAC/LTV, adoption, sales-cycle, and support signals). The intended root-cause diagnosis is withheld from this visible input; the owner intake intentionally frames the problem in the owner's own words, and the engine must trace the evidence to the true root cause without being told the answer. Not a historical case; all figures are representative.

ownerIntake.businessType: B2B wholesale marketplace connecting trade buyers with suppliers across several categories. Founded 2019, total raised $40M (Series B 2023). Monetized via a flat ~12% take-rate (commission) on GMV plus optional promotion fees. Current net revenue $7.0M (commission + fees), 30% YoY growth, GMV ~$58M annualized, ~1,400 active sellers.
ownerIntake.stage: Net revenue $7.0M, 30% YoY growth. NRR (seller net revenue retention) fell from 108% to 95%. Seller acquisition slowing. The top 8% of sellers generate 61% of GMV, and several large sellers have begun routing repeat buyers to their own direct channels after initial marketplace introduction. Take-rate is a flat ~12% regardless of seller size or order type. Cash runway 24 months.
ownerIntake.ownerGoal: Improve seller value proposition and retention, restore NRR above 105%, and slow large-seller disintermediation; reach $12M net revenue within 18 months.
ownerConstraints: Funding constraint: $40M raised, 24-month runway; the next raise is gated on GMV growth and seller retention, so large-seller GMV leakage is strategically dangerous.

Product constraint: the platform can support tiered/volume-based take-rates and value-added services (financing, logistics, buyer analytics) but these require 6-10 weeks of product+billing work to launch.
Organizational constraint: 70 staff (20 engineering, 16 seller-success/account-management, 14 buyer growth, rest G&A); account management covers large sellers but has no pricing-negotiation mandate.

Market constraint: large sellers increasingly have the scale and tooling to run direct buyer relationships once the marketplace has introduced the buyer; small/mid sellers still depend on marketplace demand generation.

Commercial constraint: a flat 12% take-rate is cheap for low-repeat, demand-dependent small sellers but expensive for high-volume, repeat-heavy large sellers whose buyers are now 'sticky' and disintermediable.
ownerIntake.immediateConcern: Seller NRR has fallen 108%→95% and the largest sellers, who drive 61% of GMV, are routing repeat buyers off-platform after the first marketplace-sourced order. The owner believes seller satisfaction and the value proposition are declining and wants to invest in seller-success headcount and new seller features. But the data shows the problem is concentrated and structural: the flat 12% take-rate is economically irrational for high-volume repeat sellers, who pay 12% on buyers the marketplace no longer needs to source, giving them a clear incentive to disintermediate. Small/mid sellers, who still depend on demand generation, are not leaving. The owner must decide within the next month whether to add seller-success resources broadly or restructure take-rate/monetization for the large-seller segment before more GMV leaks off-platform.

businessProblem: A B2B marketplace growing 30% is leaking its most valuable GMV: seller NRR fell from 108% to 95%, and the top 8% of sellers (61% of GMV) are routing repeat buyers off-platform after the first marketplace-sourced order (on-platform large-seller repeat rate fell 64%→41%, ~30% of their repeat GMV now off-platform). The owner reads this as declining seller satisfaction and value proposition and wants broad seller-success investment and new features. But the problem is concentrated and structural: a flat ~12% take-rate is cheap for demand-dependent small/mid sellers (whose retention and satisfaction are stable) and economically irrational for high-volume repeat sellers, who pay 12% on buyers the marketplace no longer sources, making disintermediation the rational move (their top complaint, 58%, is 'commission too high for repeat orders'). With the next raise gated on GMV/retention and 24 months of runway, the owner must decide whether to spread seller-success effort broadly or restructure monetization for the large-seller segment before more GMV leaks.

evidence.finding: The take-rate is a flat ~12% regardless of seller size or order type. This is structurally mispriced: it is cheap relative to value for low-repeat, demand-dependent small sellers, but expensive for high-volume repeat sellers who pay 12% on repeat buyers the marketplace no longer needs to source. The flat rate gives large sellers a direct economic incentive to disintermediate after the first order.
evidence.source: Monetization model, take-rate schedule, seller-segment revenue analysis

evidence.finding: The disintermediation is concentrated in large sellers and tied to repeat orders: large-seller on-platform repeat rate fell from 64% to 41%, and ~30% of their repeat-buyer GMV now flows off-platform. Seller NRR fell 108%→95% driven almost entirely by this leakage. Small/mid sellers' retention and repeat rates are stable.
evidence.source: GMV flow analysis, seller NRR cohort report, repeat-rate tracking

evidence.finding: Top 8% of sellers generate 61% of GMV; bottom 70% generate 14%. Large sellers now have the scale and tooling to run direct buyer relationships once the marketplace introduces the buyer, while small/mid sellers still depend on marketplace demand generation. The marketplace's value is strongest at first-order discovery and weakest at repeat for large sellers specifically.
evidence.source: Seller concentration analysis, seller capability survey

evidence.finding: Seller satisfaction is segmented: small/mid sellers report positive satisfaction, while large sellers' top complaint (58% of large-seller responses) is 'commission too high for repeat orders.' This is a monetization-structure complaint, not a generic product or service-quality complaint, localizing the cause to pricing rather than value-prop decline.
evidence.source: Seller satisfaction surveys segmented by tier

supportingData.large_seller_top_complaint: commission too high for repeat orders

evidence.finding: The buyer side is healthy: buyer demand and acquisition are stable, and the marketplace reliably delivers first-order discovery value. The leakage is not a buyer-demand failure; it is that sellers capture buyers introduced by the marketplace and route repeat business off-platform because the flat take-rate makes staying on-platform uneconomic for them.
